\chapter{A Little More Slowly}
\label{ch:ja-slower-please}
\hlchaptermodality{10}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask for slower speech, close the repair with wakarimashita, read and write the repair lines earned in the previous chapter, and write five new hiragana signs.}

A second repair strategy assembled from seven tiny lexical steps while independent reading and writing stay inside the learner's earned script boundary.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[se]{\ja{せ} — close the opener}

\label{lesson:JA-W10-se}



\begin{quote}
Ask for one repetition. Then hear the farewell in your mind, say it, read \textbf{\ja{さようなら}}, and write its final \textbf{\ja{ら}}. Write known \textbf{\ja{す}, \ja{み}, \ja{ま}, \ja{ん}} separately. Only the fourth sign of \emph{sumimasen} is still missing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{せ}} — \emph{se}
\end{quote}

Three strokes: a short horizontal, a longer crossing horizontal with a small hook, then a vertical curve through the right side. Keep the two horizontals separate.

\subsection*{Your turn}
1. Copy \textbf{\ja{せ}} once. 2. Hide it and write it after ten seconds. 3. Join the five known blocks: \textbf{\ja{す} | \ja{み} | \ja{ま} | \ja{せ} | \ja{ん}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ja{すみません}} once without romanization.

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}; stroke order per \emph{Hitsujun Shido no Tebiki} (Japanese Ministry of Education, 1958).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o]{\ja{お} — the respectful opening sign}

\label{lesson:JA-W10-o}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{onegaishimasu}, write \textbf{\ja{せ}}, then retrieve \emph{yoku} as “well.”
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{お}} — \emph{o}
\end{quote}

Three strokes. Write the short top horizontal, then the long central stroke that curves left and loops right. Finish with the small separate mark at upper right.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{\ja{お}} once
  \item \emph{Copy:} \textbf{\ja{お}} once with the model visible
  \item \emph{Find:} point to the first sign in \textbf{\ja{おねがいします}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Cover the model and air-write all three strokes.

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}; stroke order per \emph{Hitsujun Shido no Tebiki} (Japanese Ministry of Education, 1958).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ne]{\ja{ね} — finish the polite request}

\label{lesson:JA-W10-ne}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\ja{お}}, then known \textbf{\ja{が}, \ja{い}, \ja{し}, \ja{ま}, \ja{す}}. Say the whole request ending once. One written mora remains between \textbf{\ja{お}} and \textbf{\ja{が}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ね}} — \emph{ne}
\end{quote}

Two strokes. First a short vertical. Second, cross it from the upper right, hook left, sweep down, and finish with a small loop at the lower right.

\subsection*{Your turn}
1. Copy \textbf{\ja{ね}} once. 2. Hide it and write it from \emph{ne}. 3. Assemble \textbf{\ja{お} | \ja{ね} | \ja{が} | \ja{い} | \ja{し} | \ja{ま} | \ja{す}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ja{おねがいします}} without romanization, then stop.

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}; stroke order per \emph{Hitsujun Shido no Tebiki} (Japanese Ministry of Education, 1958).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sukoshi]{\ja{すこし} — ask for a small change}

\label{lesson:JA-C10-sukoshi}



\begin{quote}
Ask for one repetition, then write known \textbf{\ja{す}}, \textbf{\ja{こ}}, and \textbf{\ja{ね}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{すこし}} — \emph{su-ko-shi} — a little
\end{quote}

Three morae. This word makes a request smaller and gentler: not a completely different explanation, only \textbf{a little} adjustment. The last sign is exposure for one lesson; its own writing step comes next.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{sukoshi} $\to$ choose \textbf{a little}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{su | ko | shi}{]} {[}REPEAT x2
  \item \emph{Point to:} known \textbf{\ja{す}}, known \textbf{\ja{こ}}, supported final sign
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Keep it to three even beats.

Source: \href{https://www.irodori.jpf.go.jp/assets/data/starter/pdf/X\_L02.pdf}{Japan Foundation Irodori Starter lesson 2}, pp. 1–3.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shi]{\ja{し} — one falling curve}

\label{lesson:JA-W10-shi}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{sukoshi}. Write \textbf{\ja{す}}, \textbf{\ja{こ}}, and review \textbf{\ja{み}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{し}} — \emph{shi}
\end{quote}

One stroke. Begin high, descend almost vertically, then curve gently up and to the right. Do not add a second stroke or close the curve.

\subsection*{Your turn}
1. Trace \textbf{\ja{し}} once. 2. Hide it and write the single curve. 3. Join \textbf{\ja{す} | \ja{こ} | \ja{し}} and read the three morae.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ja{すこし}} once without support.

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}; stroke order per \emph{Hitsujun Shido no Tebiki} (Japanese Ministry of Education, 1958).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yukkuri]{\ja{ゆっくり} — slowly, with a held beat}

\label{lesson:JA-C10-yukkuri}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ja{すこし}}, then write known \textbf{\ja{く}}, \textbf{\ja{り}}, and \textbf{\ja{し}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ゆっくり}} — \emph{yu-k-ku-ri} — slowly
\end{quote}

Do not squeeze the middle. The small \textbf{\ja{っ}} holds one beat of closure before \emph{ku}. The spelling is exposure today; this lesson earns the sound and practical job without pretending the two new shapes are already readable.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{yukkuri} $\to$ choose \textbf{slowly}
  \item \emph{Tap:} \emph{yu | hold | ku | ri}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yukkuri} slowly, without adding a vowel in the held beat
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Meaning and timing are enough. The new opening sign comes next.

Source: \href{https://www.irodori.jpf.go.jp/assets/data/starter/pdf/X\_L02.pdf}{Japan Foundation Irodori Starter lesson 2}, pp. 1–3.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yu]{\ja{ゆ} — open yukkuri}

\label{lesson:JA-W10-yu}



\begin{quote}
Tap \emph{yu | hold | ku | ri}, then write known \textbf{\ja{よ}} and \textbf{\ja{も}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ゆ}} — \emph{yu}
\end{quote}

Two strokes. First a short curved vertical on the left. Second, begin at the upper right, sweep left through the middle, loop around, and finish to the right.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{\ja{ゆ}} once
  \item \emph{Copy:} \textbf{\ja{ゆ}} once
  \item \emph{Find:} point to \textbf{\ja{ゆ}} at the start of \textbf{\ja{ゆっくり}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The small \textbf{\ja{っ}} remains supported; do not decode past what you own.

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}; stroke order per \emph{Hitsujun Shido no Tebiki} (Japanese Ministry of Education, 1958).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[itte kudasai]{\ja{いってください} — please say it}

\label{lesson:JA-C10-itte-kudasai}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{yukkuri}. Retrieve \emph{onegaishimasu}, then write \textbf{\ja{い}, \ja{く}, \ja{さ}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{いってください。}} — \emph{itte kudasai} — please say it
\end{quote}

The first part is the request-linking form of \emph{iu}, “to say.” \emph{Kudasai} makes the requested action polite. Learn the whole spoken frame now. Its small \textbf{\ja{っ}}, \textbf{\ja{て}}, and voiced \textbf{\ja{だ}} receive separate writing steps later.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{itte kudasai} $\to$ choose \textbf{please say it}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{it-te ku-da-sa-i}
  \item \emph{Join:} \emph{yukkuri itte kudasai} — please say it slowly
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Do not write the supported signs from memory yet.

Source: \href{https://www.irodori.jpf.go.jp/assets/data/starter/pdf/X\_L02.pdf}{Japan Foundation Irodori Starter lesson 2}, pp. 1–3.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mō sukoshi]{\ja{もうすこし} — a little more}

\label{lesson:JA-C10-mou-sukoshi}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{itte kudasai}, write \textbf{\ja{ゆ}}, then write \textbf{\ja{もう}} and \textbf{\ja{すこし}} separately. Read both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{もうすこし}} — \emph{mō sukoshi} — a little more
\end{quote}

No new grammar is hiding here. \textbf{\ja{もう}} points beyond the present amount; \textbf{\ja{すこし}} keeps the requested change small. Every sign is already earned.

\subsection*{Your turn}
1. Read \textbf{\ja{もう} | \ja{すこし}}. 2. Say \emph{mō sukoshi}, keeping the extra beat in \textbf{\ja{もう}}. 3. Hear the phrase, wait ten seconds, and write it from memory.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Circle \textbf{\ja{う}}, the second beat of \emph{mō}.

Source: \href{https://www.irodori.jpf.go.jp/assets/data/starter/pdf/X\_L02.pdf}{Japan Foundation Irodori Starter lesson 2}, pp. 1–3.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wakarimashita]{\ja{わかりました} — the repair worked}

\label{lesson:JA-C10-wakarimashita}



\begin{quote}
Say “I do not understand,” then read \textbf{\ja{もうすこし}}. Write \textbf{\ja{み}} and \textbf{\ja{し}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{わかりました。}} — \emph{wakarimashita} — I understand; understood
\end{quote}

The familiar \emph{wakari-} stem returns. Polite \emph{-mashita} presents the change as achieved: the explanation landed. The final \textbf{\ja{た}} is supported exposure until its own sign lesson.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{wakarimasen} $\to$ not understood
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{wakarimashita} $\to$ understood now
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{wakarimashita} after a successful repetition
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Keep \emph{-masen} and \emph{-mashita} distinct; one reports a problem, the other success.

Source: \href{https://www.irodori.jpf.go.jp/assets/data/starter/pdf/X\_L02.pdf}{Japan Foundation Irodori Starter lesson 2}, pp. 2–3.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[koko]{\ja{ここ} — here, with one known sign twice}

\label{lesson:JA-C10-koko}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\ja{こ}}, say \emph{wakarimashita}, then retrieve \emph{sumimasen}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ここ}} — \emph{ko-ko} — here; this place
\end{quote}

One owned sign appears twice. The word belongs to a larger pointing family that will later contrast near me, near you, and over there. Today, keep only the speaker-near place: \textbf{here}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
1. Point beside yourself and say \emph{koko}. 2. Read \textbf{\ja{こ} | \ja{こ}}. 3. Hear \emph{ko-ko}, wait ten seconds, and write both signs.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
No new shape was needed; the payoff is recombination.

Source: \href{https://www.irodori.jpf.go.jp/assets/data/starter/pdf/X\_L02.pdf}{Japan Foundation Irodori Starter lesson 2}, p. 2.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mō sukoshi, yukkuri itte kudasai]{\ja{もうすこし、ゆっくりいってください} — slower, please}

\label{lesson:JA-C10-slower-please}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\ja{せ}, \ja{お}, \ja{ね}, \ja{し}, \ja{ゆ}}. Read \emph{sumimasen} and \emph{onegaishimasu}. Retrieve the repetition request, then the three new spoken pieces \emph{mō sukoshi}, \emph{yukkuri}, and \emph{itte kudasai}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{もうすこし、ゆっくりいってください。}}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{mō sukoshi, yukkuri itte kudasai} — please say it a little more slowly
\end{quote}

No new rule arrives here. The first block is independently readable and writable. The second and third remain sound-first exposure where their small \textbf{\ja{っ}}, \textbf{\ja{て}}, and \textbf{\ja{だ}} have not yet received individual writing lessons.

\subsection*{Your turn}
1. \textbf{Listen:} choose repetition or slower speech from the request you hear. 2. \textbf{Speak:} \emph{sumimasen} + the slower request. 3. \textbf{Read/write:} independently retrieve only \textbf{\ja{もうすこし}}. 4. \textbf{Close:} after the repeated line, say \emph{wakarimashita}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Stop after one accurate repair and one \emph{wakarimashita}.

Source: \href{https://www.irodori.jpf.go.jp/assets/data/starter/pdf/X\_L02.pdf}{Japan Foundation Irodori Starter lesson 2}, pp. 1–3.
\end{tcolorbox}
